title: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
summary: How Windows really decides who can do what: SIDs, tokens, UAC, ACLs, services, LSASS, the registry and event logs, then SMB, RDP, patching and domains through WannaCry, NotPetya, BlueKeep and PrintNightmare.
outcomes: Read a SID and an access token and explain how the access check walks a DACL to allow or deny
Explain UAC's split token and integrity levels, and read Token Elevation Type in event 4688
Explain why attackers target LSASS and services, and which protections and events stop or reveal them
Find persistence in Run keys, services and scheduled tasks with read-only PowerShell
Interpret key event IDs (4624 logon types, 4625, 4688, 4720, 4732, 4698, 7045, 4104, 1102) as a sequence
Explain how WannaCry, NotPetya, BlueKeep and PrintNightmare exploited SMB, credentials, RDP and the spooler
Describe what domains, domain controllers, Kerberos and Group Policy add on top of a single machine

lessons.title: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows

blocks.md:
You use Windows every day, but as a defender you need to see what it does underneath. Start with one tiny action: Ana signs in to a work laptop and double-clicks `report.docx`.

In that second, six Windows parts each played a role: an **account** proved who Ana is, a **process** started Word, a **token** carried Ana's identity into that process, a **file permission** check decided whether Word may open the file, and the **registry** supplied Word's settings. If auditing is on, an **event log** wrote down some of it. This course takes those parts one at a time, then shows how attackers abuse each one and what defenders see.

blocks.title: One double-click, six Windows parts

scenes.caption: Ana types a password. LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, the Windows process that checks sign-ins) verifies it.
After a successful check Windows builds an access token: Ana's SIDs (security identifiers) and privileges. Every process started for Ana gets a copy.
explorer.exe, the desktop shell, runs with that token. When Ana double-clicks, Explorer starts Word, and Word inherits the token.
Word asks to open the file. Windows compares the token with the file's ACL (access control list) and allows or denies. Word also reads its settings from the registry.
If the audit policy says so, Windows records the sign-in, the new process and the file access in the Security event log. That record is what a defender reads later.

blocks.md:
Every attack on a Windows machine is a story about these same parts. Attackers want to:

1. **Get in** as some account (a stolen password, a vulnerable network service).
2. **Climb** from a normal user to an administrator or to SYSTEM, the all-powerful built-in identity Windows itself runs as.
3. **Stay** by making their program start again after a reboot (registry Run keys, services, scheduled tasks).
4. **Move** to other machines (file sharing over SMB, Remote Desktop).
5. **Hide**, for example by clearing the event logs.

The defender's job is to answer three questions from the evidence: **who** (which account), **what** (which process, with which command line) and **when and where** (time and machine). Windows answers them through SIDs, tokens and event logs.

Windows security is identity attached to processes. A process acts with the token it was given, so "which account ran this, and with which token" is the first question in almost every Windows investigation.

You will run small, read-only commands throughout. Open **PowerShell** (Microsoft's command shell; the next lesson explains it) from the Start menu and try the commands below. `whoami` ("who am I") prints the account the shell runs as, and its switches show the SID, the groups in your token and your privileges.

blocks.code:
PS C:\> whoami
laptop01\ana
PS C:\> whoami /user        # your account name and SID
PS C:\> whoami /groups      # every group SID in your token
PS C:\> whoami /priv        # privileges in your token
PS C:\> hostname            # the computer's name
blocks.caption: Read-only commands. Output is shortened; your names will differ.

blocks.md: Practise only on machines you own or are allowed to test, ideally a Windows virtual machine you created. The legal line from security-basics applies to every command and tool in this course.

blocks.question: Ana's Word process opens a file. Whose identity does Windows check against the file's permissions?
options: The identity of whoever installed Word
The SIDs in the access token that Word inherited from Explorer, which came from Ana's sign-in
The computer's identity, because files belong to the computer
No identity: local files are always readable by local programs
blocks.explain: A process acts with its token. Word got a copy of Ana's token when Explorer started it, so the access check compares the file's ACL with Ana's user and group SIDs. Who installed the program does not matter.

blocks.question: Which attacker goal does clearing the Security event log serve?
options: Getting in
Climbing to administrator
Hiding
Moving to other machines
blocks.explain: Clearing logs removes evidence. Windows records a separate event (1102) when the Security log is cleared, which you will meet in the event log lessons.

lessons.title: PowerShell: objects in a pipeline, and why attackers like it

blocks.md:
**PowerShell** is Microsoft's task automation tool: a command-line shell, a scripting language and a configuration framework in one, and it runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. Its commands are called **cmdlets** (pronounced command-lets: small built-in commands, as opposed to separate programs). Cmdlet names follow a **Verb-Noun** pattern: `Get-Process` gets processes, `Stop-Service` stops a service, `Get-WinEvent` gets Windows events.

Tiny example: `Get-Process` lists running programs. You do not need to memorise names: `Get-Command -Noun Process` lists every cmdlet whose noun is Process, and `Get-Help` explains any of them.

The big difference from older shells: most shells pass **text** from one command to the next, but PowerShell passes **.NET objects** (.NET is Microsoft's software platform that PowerShell is built on; its objects are structured records with named properties such as `Name`, `Id` and `Status`). The `|` character is the **pipeline**: each command receives the objects the previous one emitted. So you filter with property names instead of cutting columns out of text.

blocks.title: Objects flowing through a pipeline
blocks.code:
Get-Service |
  Where-Object Status -eq 'Running' |
  Select-Object -First 3 Name, StartType

scenes.caption: Get-Service emits one object per installed service. Each object has properties such as Name and Status. The count is an example machine.
Where-Object keeps only objects whose Status property equals Running. No text parsing happened: the shell compared a property.
Select-Object keeps 3 objects and only 2 properties. The objects are still structured, so the next command could sort or export them.

scenes.output:
Name     StartType
----     ---------
Appinfo                 Manual
AudioEndpointBuilder Automatic
Audiosrv             Automatic
scenes.caption: Only at the end does PowerShell format the objects as a table for your screen. The output shown is illustrative.

blocks.code:
Get-Command -Noun Process              # which cmdlets deal with processes?
Get-Help Get-WinEvent -Examples        # worked examples for a cmdlet
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, Id, CPU
Get-LocalUser                          # local accounts (next lesson)
blocks.caption: Everyday read-only commands you will reuse in later lessons.

blocks.md:
**Why attackers use PowerShell.** It is already installed, it can reach almost every part of Windows, and it can download and run code. MITRE ATT&CK, a public catalogue of attacker techniques, lists it as [technique T1059.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/) and notes it can run downloaded code in memory without writing a file to disk. That makes file-based antivirus alone a weak defence.

**What defenders have:**
- **AMSI** (Antimalware Scan Interface): a Windows interface that lets PowerShell hand script content to the installed antivirus for scanning before it runs, including code built at run time.
- **Script block logging**: when turned on by Group Policy (Windows' way to push settings to many machines, last lesson) or the registry (lesson 9), PowerShell records the content of every script block it processes as **event 4104** in the `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational` log. Even obfuscated commands must be turned back into code before they run, and that is what gets logged.

blocks.prompt: A company sets the PowerShell execution policy to Restricted on every laptop and calls PowerShell "locked down". A user who cannot run a `.ps1` script file copies the script's text and pastes it into the console. What happens?
blocks.reveal: It runs. Microsoft's own documentation says the execution policy **is not a security boundary**: "users can easily bypass a policy by typing the script contents at the command line". The execution policy is a safety catch against running scripts by accident, not a control against a determined user or attacker. Real controls are application control, AMSI with an antivirus, and script block logging so you can see what ran.

blocks.md: Misconception: "execution policy stops malicious PowerShell". It does not. Treat it as a seat belt for honest users, and rely on logging, AMSI and application control for security.

blocks.code:
# Read-only: is script block logging turned on by policy? (1 = on)
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -Name EnableScriptBlockLogging

# Read the most recent logged script blocks (event 4104)
# (-MaxEvents applies before Where-Object, so filter in the query instead)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational'; Id=4104} -MaxEvents 20

# Even with the policy unset, PowerShell 5+ logs script blocks that look
# malicious (Warning level); setting the policy to Disabled turns that off.
blocks.caption: Windows PowerShell 5.1 logs to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational. PowerShell 7 logs to a separate PowerShellCore/Operational log.

blocks.md: Script logs can capture secrets that scripts handle. Microsoft recommends Protected Event Logging, which encrypts that content with a public key so only the central log collector holding the private key can read it.

blocks.question: Why does PowerShell filtering use `Where-Object Status -eq 'Running'` rather than searching the text of each line?
options: Because the pipeline carries objects with named properties, so you compare a property directly
Because PowerShell has no text search
Because Status is a keyword of the shell
Because Where-Object only works on services
blocks.explain: Cmdlets emit .NET objects. Each has properties you can compare, sort and select, which is more reliable than matching text that might change format.

blocks.question: An attacker runs an obfuscated PowerShell command that decodes itself in memory and never touches disk. Which defender data source is most likely to show the actual code that ran?
options: The PowerShell execution policy setting
The list of installed programs
The NTFS permissions on powershell.exe
Script block logging (event 4104)
blocks.explain: Script block logging records the code PowerShell actually processes, after decoding. The execution policy is not a security boundary and records nothing.

lessons.title: Accounts, groups and SIDs: how Windows names every identity

blocks.md:
An **account** is an identity Windows can authenticate: a person (Ana), a computer, or a service. A **group** is a named set of accounts, so permissions can be given once to the group rather than to each person. On a standalone computer the accounts live in a local database run by the **SAM** (Security Accounts Manager), stored in a protected part of the registry. In a company network they usually live in Active Directory instead (last lesson).

Tiny example: Ana's laptop has a local account `ana`. Ana is a member of the local **Administrators** group, so Ana can change system settings.

Windows does not track accounts by name, because names can be renamed. It uses a **SID** (security identifier): a unique, never-reused number issued when the account or group is created. Written as text, a SID looks like `S-1-5-21-1377283216-344919071-3415362939-500`:

- `S` says this is a SID; `1` is the revision (format version).
- `5` is the **identifier authority**, here NT Authority (the Windows security authority). `1` would be the World Authority, used by the Everyone group.
- The middle numbers (`21-...-3415362939`) are the **domain identifier**: they identify the computer or domain that issued the SID.
- The last number is the **RID** (relative identifier, relative because it is unique only within that domain). RID 500 is always the built-in Administrator account.

blocks.title: Reading a SID piece by piece

scenes.caption: A local account SID from Microsoft's sample event: the built-in Administrator of computer WIN-GG82ULGC9GO. Domain parts are shortened to fit.
S, then revision 1, then identifier authority 5 (NT Authority). Almost every account SID you see starts S-1-5.
21 plus three large numbers form the domain identifier: unique to this computer (or domain). No two domains in one enterprise share it.
The last value is the RID. 500 always means the built-in Administrator, even if someone renames the account, so renaming does not hide it.
Built-in groups use domain identifier 32 (Builtin), which is the same on every computer. S-1-5-32-544 is the Administrators group everywhere.

blocks.md:
Identities you will meet constantly:

- **Administrator** (RID 500): the built-in admin account. Windows setup **disables** it and creates another local account in the Administrators group instead. It cannot be deleted or removed from Administrators.
- **Guest** (RID 501): an account for people without their own. It does not require a password, so it should stay disabled.
- **Administrators** (`S-1-5-32-544`): members get full control of the machine.
- **SYSTEM** (`S-1-5-18`, also called LocalSystem): the identity the operating system and many services run as. It is a hidden member of Administrators and has full control of files on NTFS volumes. On the network it acts as the computer itself.
- **LOCAL SERVICE** (`S-1-5-19`) and **NETWORK SERVICE** (`S-1-5-20`): weaker service identities. LOCAL SERVICE has ordinary user rights locally and is anonymous on the network; NETWORK SERVICE uses the computer's identity on the network.
- **Everyone** (`S-1-1-0`): every user.

blocks.code:
Get-LocalUser | Select-Object Name, Enabled, SID     # local accounts and their SIDs
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'         # who is a local admin?
whoami /user                                          # my own SID
blocks.caption: Read-only. Audit the Administrators group regularly: every member can do anything on the machine.

blocks.md: SIDs, not names, are what Windows checks. A renamed Administrator still has RID 500, and a deleted and re-created account gets a new SID, so it does not inherit the old account's permissions.

**Defender view.** Local admin accounts are a favourite target. If many laptops share the same local admin password, stealing it on one machine opens all of them. Microsoft's **LAPS** (Local Administrator Password Solution) fixes this by giving each device its own rotating local admin password, stored centrally. Watch for new members of Administrators (event 4732, later lesson) and keep that group small.

blocks.question: An admin renames the built-in Administrator account to `support` to hide it from attackers. Why does this give little protection?
options: Renaming is undone at every reboot
The account keeps RID 500 in its SID, and tools can look up accounts by SID
Windows refuses to rename that account
Attackers only ever guess the name Guest
blocks.explain: Microsoft notes a renamed Administrator keeps the same SID ending in 500, which attackers can discover. Disabling the account and using LAPS for local admin passwords are the real defences.

blocks.question: Ana's account is deleted and re-created with the same name `ana`. Ana cannot open folders Ana used to own. Why?
options: The new account has a new SID, and the folders' permissions name the old SID
Folder permissions expire after 90 days
Re-created accounts are always Guests
The SAM caches the old password
blocks.explain: Permissions store SIDs. SIDs are never reused, so the new account is a different security principal and the old grants do not apply to it.

lessons.title: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no

blocks.md:
When Ana signs in and the password checks out, Windows builds an **access token**: an object describing the security context of a process. It holds Ana's user SID, the SIDs of every group Ana belongs to, a **logon SID** for this sign-in session, a list of **privileges** (system-wide powers such as backing up any file or debugging any process), and a few defaults. Every process started for Ana gets a copy.

Tiny example: `whoami /groups` on Ana's laptop shows `BUILTIN\Users`, `Everyone` and (if Ana is an admin) `BUILTIN\Administrators`. Those exact SIDs are what get compared with file permissions.

Every **securable object** (file, folder, registry key, service, process) carries a **security descriptor**: its owner SID, plus a **DACL** (discretionary access control list: who may do what, discretionary because the object's owner decides who gets access) and a **SACL** (system access control list: which access attempts the system should audit). A DACL is a list of **ACEs** (access control entries). Each ACE names one trustee SID and either allows or denies some rights.

The **access check** walks the DACL from the top and stops at the first of three outcomes:
1. An access-denied ACE matches a SID in the token and denies any requested right: **denied**.
2. Allow ACEs that match the token have together granted every requested right: **granted**.
3. The list ends with some requested right never granted: **denied** (implicitly).

blocks.title: The access check walks the DACL in order

scenes.caption: A folder's DACL with three ACEs: deny Bob everything, allow the Sales group to write, allow Users to read. Order matters.
Bob (member of Sales and Users) asks to read. ACE 1 names Bob and denies: the check stops at once. Bob is denied even though ACE 3 would allow read.
Ana (Sales and Users) asks for read and write. ACE 1 is not about Ana, skip. ACE 2 grants write. Still missing read, keep going.
ACE 3 grants read. Every requested right is now granted, so access is granted and the walk stops.
Kim (only in Users) asks to write. ACE 1 and 2 do not match Kim. ACE 3 only gives read. The list ends with write never granted: implicitly denied.

blocks.caption: Simplified model of the documented algorithm in Python. Real Windows also checks integrity labels first (next lesson), ignores disabled group SIDs and handles special rights.

blocks.prompt: An object has a DACL that contains zero ACEs. Another object has no DACL at all. Which one can everybody open?
blocks.reveal: The object with **no DACL**: Windows grants full access to everyone. The object with an **empty DACL** denies everyone, because no ACE ever grants anything and the check ends in an implicit deny. Mixing these two up is a classic configuration bug: a "null DACL" is wide open.

blocks.md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

**Privileges are not permissions.** Permissions live on objects (the DACL). Privileges live in the token and apply system-wide. For example `SeDebugPrivilege` lets a process debug and adjust the memory of processes owned by other accounts, and `SeBackupPrivilege` grants read access to any file regardless of its ACL, for backups. That is why attackers who reach administrator often enable the debug privilege, and why Windows logs **event 4672** (special privileges assigned to a new logon) whenever an account with such powers signs in.

blocks.question: A folder's DACL is: (1) Allow Users: Read, (2) Deny Interns: Read. Intern Sam is in both Users and Interns and asks to read. What happens?
options: Denied, because deny always wins regardless of order
Denied implicitly, because two ACEs conflict
Granted, because ACE 1 grants every requested right and the walk stops before the deny
Granted only if Sam is an administrator
blocks.explain: The access check stops as soon as all requested rights are granted. ACE 1 grants read, so the deny is never reached. This is why the canonical order puts explicit denies first.

blocks.question: Which of these is a privilege (in the token) rather than a permission (in an object's DACL)?
options: Read access on the Reports folder for the Sales group
Deny Write on a registry key for Guests
Full control on a service for Administrators
Debug programs (SeDebugPrivilege)
blocks.explain: Privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege are listed in the access token and apply across the system. The others are ACEs on particular objects.

lessons.title: UAC and integrity levels: why admins do not run as admin

blocks.md:
If Ana is an administrator, should every program Ana runs, including a web browser and a malicious attachment, get full admin rights? Windows says no. **UAC** (User Account Control) limits the ability of programs to run with administrator rights unless the user approves.

Tiny example: Ana, an admin, opens the Date and Time settings. Changing the time zone works straight away. The "Change date and time" button has a **shield icon**: changing the system clock needs the full admin token, so Windows asks first.

**How it works.** When an administrator signs in, Windows creates **two tokens**: a full **administrator token** and a **filtered standard-user token**: admin privileges are removed and the Administrators SID is kept but marked **deny only**, so it can match a deny ACE but never grants access. That is why `whoami /groups` in a normal window still lists `BUILTIN\Administrators`, as "Group used for deny only". Explorer runs with the filtered one, and every program Ana starts inherits it. When a program needs admin rights, Windows shows an **elevation prompt**:
- a **consent prompt** (Yes or No) for admins in Admin Approval Mode (the default UAC mode, where an admin works with the filtered token until approving),
- a **credential prompt** (type an admin's password) for standard users.

The prompt appears on the **secure desktop**, a separate desktop only Windows processes can reach, so ordinary malware cannot click Yes for you.

blocks.title: One sign-in, two tokens, one elevation

scenes.caption: Ana is in Administrators, so the logon creates a full admin token and a filtered standard token.
Explorer gets the filtered token. Every program Ana starts from the desktop inherits it, so it runs as a standard user.
The installer declares that it needs administrator rights, so it cannot simply inherit the filtered token.
Windows switches to the secure desktop and shows the consent prompt with the program's publisher.
Only after Ana clicks Yes does setup.exe start with the full administrator token at high integrity.

blocks.md:
**Integrity levels** are a second, separate check called **Mandatory Integrity Control**. Every token and every object carries an integrity label, written as a SID under authority 16. Standard users run at **medium**, elevated programs at **high**, system services at **system**, and sandboxed programs (some browser processes) at **low**. Objects without a label count as medium.

The default rule is **no write up**: a process cannot write to an object with a higher integrity level, even if the DACL would allow it. This check happens **before** the DACL check. A new process gets the lower of the user's level and the program file's level, so even an admin running a low-integrity program gets a low-integrity process.

blocks.title: Integrity levels are numbers (the RID of the label SID)

scenes.caption: The label SIDs are S-1-16 followed by these RIDs: 0x1000 = 4096 (low), 0x2000 = 8192 (medium), 0x3000 = 12288 (high), 0x4000 = 16384 (system).
Ana's Explorer and Word run at medium (S-1-16-8192), including for admins using the filtered token.
A low-integrity process cannot write to Ana's medium-integrity files, even if their DACL says Users may write. No write up.
Elevated admin programs run at high; services as SYSTEM run at system. Event 4688 records the level given to each new process.

blocks.code:
PS C:\> whoami /groups | Select-String 'Mandatory'
Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level   Label   S-1-16-8192

# The same check from an elevated (Run as administrator) window:
Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level     Label   S-1-16-12288
blocks.caption: Abridged output. The integrity level of your shell is listed among the token's groups.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.** The Security log's process creation event (4688) has a **Token Elevation Type** field:
- `%%1936` (type 1): full token, used when UAC is off or for the built-in Administrator, services and SYSTEM. Microsoft suggests alerting when a real user account shows type 1, because it usually means UAC is disabled for that account.
- `%%1937` (type 2): elevated token, the user chose Run as administrator or the program always asks for admin.
- `%%1938` (type 3): limited (filtered) token, the normal case.

Attackers who get code running as a medium-integrity admin often try a **UAC bypass**: a trick to reach high integrity without the prompt (ATT&CK [T1548.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/002/)). The defence is to make daily accounts standard users, which Microsoft recommends, and to keep the prompt on the secure desktop. UAC is defence in depth, not a security boundary: Microsoft does not promise to fix bypasses. Its successor, **Administrator protection** (off by default, on in the October 2026 baselines) uses a hidden admin account and Windows Hello.

blocks.question: Ana is in Administrators with UAC on. Ana double-clicks a downloaded tool that does not ask for elevation. Which Token Elevation Type will its 4688 event show?
options: %%1936, a full token, because Ana is an admin
%%1938, a limited token
%%1937, an elevated token
No 4688 event is written for admins
blocks.explain: Programs started from Explorer inherit the filtered token unless they request elevation and the user approves. The limited token is type 3, logged as %%1938.

blocks.question: A low-integrity browser process tries to modify a file in Ana's Documents folder. The file's DACL allows Ana full control. What happens?
options: Allowed, because the DACL allows Ana
Allowed only after a UAC prompt
Blocked, because the integrity check runs before the DACL and forbids writing up to medium
Blocked, because browsers have no token
blocks.explain: Mandatory Integrity Control is evaluated before the DACL. A low-integrity token cannot write to a medium (or unlabeled) object, whatever the DACL says.

lessons.title: NTFS permissions and inheritance: reading and fixing an ACL

blocks.md:
**NTFS** is the default Windows file system (it arrived with Windows NT). Among its features are security descriptors on every file and folder, so each one has an owner and a DACL you can read.

Tiny example: `icacls C:\Reports` prints the folder's DACL as one line per ACE: a SID's name, some inheritance flags in brackets, and the rights. `icacls` is the built-in tool that displays and changes DACLs (and integrity labels); it replaced the older, deprecated `cacls`.

blocks.code:
PS C:\> icacls C:\Reports
C:\Reports BUILTIN\Administrators:(OI)(CI)(F)
           NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(F)
           CONTOSO\Sales:(OI)(CI)(M)
           BUILTIN\Users:(OI)(CI)(RX)
Successfully processed 1 files; Failed processing 0 files
blocks.caption: Illustrative output. F full, M modify, RX read and execute, R read, W write, D delete, N no access.

blocks.md:
How to read the flags:
- **(OI)** object inherit: files inside this folder inherit the ACE.
- **(CI)** container inherit: subfolders inherit the ACE.
- **(IO)** inherit only: the ACE applies to children, not to this folder itself.
- **(I)** inherited: this ACE was copied down from a parent folder rather than set here.

**Inheritance** is why you rarely set permissions file by file: set them on a folder and they flow to everything below. It is also why one bad grant high up the tree can expose thousands of files.

blocks.title: Inheritance: one ACE flows down the tree

scenes.caption: An admin grants Sales Modify on the Reports folder with (OI)(CI), so both files and subfolders will inherit it.
The subfolder 2026-Q1 inherits the ACE (shown with the (I) flag). The admin did not touch it.
Files inherit it too. Every Sales member can now change the budget sheet.
The SACL is separate: if auditing is on for this folder, a write by a Sales member can produce event 4663 in the Security log.

blocks.md: **A real bug class: writable service binaries.** A service is a program Windows starts in the background, often as SYSTEM (lesson 7). If ordinary users can modify the folder or the `.exe` a SYSTEM service runs, any user can replace the program, and the next time the service starts, their code runs as SYSTEM. MITRE ATT&CK lists this as [Services File Permissions Weakness (T1574.010)](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/010/). It usually comes from an installer that sets loose permissions on its own folder.

blocks.code:
# VULNERABLE: the AcmeAgent service runs as LocalSystem from this folder,
# and an installer granted every user Modify on it (explicit ACE).
PS C:\> icacls "C:\Program Files\AcmeAgent"
C:\Program Files\AcmeAgent BUILTIN\Users:(OI)(CI)(M)
                           NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(F)
                           BUILTIN\Administrators:(OI)(CI)(F)

# FIXED: replace the Users grant with read and execute only.
# /grant:r replaces the explicit rights previously granted to that SID.
PS C:\> icacls "C:\Program Files\AcmeAgent" /grant:r "BUILTIN\Users:(OI)(CI)(RX)"
blocks.caption: AcmeAgent is a made-up product. Run the fix only on your own lab machine.

blocks.md: **Why the fix works.** With Modify, any user could overwrite `agent.exe`. With only RX (read and execute), users can still run and read the program but cannot change it, so the SYSTEM service only ever runs code an administrator placed there. Prevention: check permissions on every service path when software is installed. Detection: Sysmon (a free logging tool, lesson 12) event 11 (file created or overwritten) showing a service binary written by a non-admin account, followed by a restart of that service.

blocks.question: A folder shows `CONTOSO\Sales:(I)(OI)(CI)(M)`. An admin runs `icacls` on that folder to remove Sales and it reports success, but Sales still has access. What is the most likely reason?
options: The ACE is inherited (I) from a parent folder, so it must be changed on the parent or inheritance broken here
icacls cannot remove groups
Sales is a built-in group that cannot be removed
The change applies only after a reboot
blocks.explain: (I) means the ACE was inherited. Removing explicit ACEs here does not touch it. Change the parent folder's ACL, or disable inheritance on this folder.

blocks.question: Why does a writable folder for a SYSTEM service turn any user into SYSTEM?
options: SYSTEM reads the user's token when it starts
Writable folders automatically grant SeDebugPrivilege
NTFS treats write as full control
The user can replace the program the service runs, and the service runs whatever is in that file with its own SYSTEM token
blocks.explain: The service's token is SYSTEM no matter who wrote the file. Control the file and you control what code runs with that token.

lessons.title: Processes, services and svchost: what runs, and as whom

blocks.md:
A **process** is a running program with its own resources: a private memory space (virtual address space), its code, open handles to objects, a **security context** (its token), a unique **PID** (process identifier) and at least one **thread** (the unit Windows actually schedules on a CPU). One program file can run as many processes.

Tiny example: open Task Manager's Details tab. `explorer.exe` is your desktop; `winword.exe` is Word; you will see many copies of `svchost.exe` and one `lsass.exe`. Every row has a PID and a user name: that user name comes from the process token.

A **service** is a program that Windows starts in the background, often at boot, with no user signed in. The **SCM** (service control manager) starts at boot, keeps the database of installed services, starts and stops them, and is an **RPC server** (remote procedure call: a way for one machine to call functions on another), so services can be managed across the network. Each service is configured with a binary path and an account to run as, usually LocalSystem, LOCAL SERVICE or NETWORK SERVICE.

Many Windows services are not separate programs but DLLs (dynamic-link libraries, code files loaded into a process). **svchost.exe** (Service Host) is the shell process that loads them. Services with matching security needs share a host group, and on machines with more than 3.5 GB of RAM, Windows 10 version 1703 and later give most services their own svchost process. That is why you see dozens of them.

blocks.title: The service control manager and the accounts services run as

scenes.caption: At boot the SCM reads its service database and starts services. Each has an account; the account becomes the token of the service process.
Three svchost.exe instances, each running services as a different account: SYSTEM (all-powerful), NETWORK SERVICE and LOCAL SERVICE (both with ordinary local rights).
LSASS, which checks sign-ins and holds credential material, also runs as SYSTEM. It is the next lesson's focus.
A third-party service, here AcmeAgent, also runs as LocalSystem. Every SYSTEM service is a possible path to full control if it is buggy or its files are writable.
An attacker with admin rights, locally or over RPC from another machine, can install a new service. The System log records event 7045.

blocks.code:
# Which services run, as which account, from which file?
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
  Select-Object Name, State, StartName, PathName |
  Sort-Object StartName

# How many svchost processes, and are they all from System32?
Get-Process -Name svchost | Select-Object Id, Path
blocks.caption: Read-only. Run elevated: without admin rights Path is blank for processes of other accounts, including most svchost.exe. StartName is the service account; PathName is the command line the SCM runs. A svchost.exe outside the System32 folder deserves a close look.

blocks.md:
**Why attackers love services.** A service runs as a powerful account and starts automatically, so creating one gives both privilege and persistence (ATT&CK [T1543.003](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/)). Remote administration tools such as PsExec (a tool that runs commands on other machines, from Sysinternals, Microsoft's free collection of Windows utilities, a site created in 1996 by Mark Russinovich, a Windows internals expert) work by copying a program to the target and installing it as a service named PSEXESVC. JPCERT/CC, Japan's computer emergency response team, documents that on the target this leaves [event 7045 in the System log](https://jpcertcc.github.io/ToolAnalysisResultSheet/details/PsExec.htm), "A service was installed in the system", with the service name, account and file path.

**Parent and child processes** are the other big signal. Every process has a creator. Word starting `powershell.exe` is unusual; a Security log 4688 event records both the new process and its creator, so defenders can spot odd pairs.
For every unknown process or service ask: which account (token), which file path, which parent, and when was it created? Those four facts come from Task Manager, Get-CimInstance, 4688 and 7045.

blocks.question: A new service appears on a file server: name `UpdSvc`, account LocalSystem, path `C:\Users\Public\u.exe`, and a 7045 event from 02:14. Which detail is the strongest red flag?
options: It runs as LocalSystem
Its binary sits in a user-writable public folder rather than Program Files or System32
Its name is short
It was logged in the System log
blocks.explain: Many legitimate services run as LocalSystem. A SYSTEM service whose binary lives in a folder any user can write combines the service persistence trick with the writable-binary bug from the last lesson.

blocks.question: Why does a typical Windows 10 or 11 machine show dozens of svchost.exe processes?
options: svchost hosts DLL-based services, and on machines with more than 3.5 GB of RAM most services get their own svchost instance
Each is a different malware family
Each user tab in a browser starts one
Windows starts one per CPU core
blocks.explain: Since Windows 10 version 1703, grouped services are split into separate svchost processes when the machine has more than 3.5 GB of RAM, for reliability and isolation.

lessons.title: LSASS: why attackers dump its memory, and how Windows protects it

blocks.md:
The **LSA** (Local Security Authority) validates users for local and remote sign-ins and enforces local security policy. Its process is **lsass.exe**, the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service. So that you are not asked for your password again for every file share or mail server (**single sign-on**), Windows keeps credential material for signed-in users in LSASS memory: for example NTLM password hashes (NTLM, NT LAN Manager, is Windows' older sign-in protocol, explained below) and Kerberos tickets (the domain sign-in protocol of the last lesson).

Tiny example: Ana signs in at 09:00 and opens a network share at 09:05 without typing a password again. Something had to remember a proof of Ana's identity. That something is LSASS.

A **hash** (recall from security-basics) is a fixed-size fingerprint of data. Windows NTLM authentication (a challenge-response family of protocols that grew out of the older LAN Manager) proves knowledge of the password by using its hash, so the hash itself works like the password. That gives **pass the hash**: authenticating as a user with only the stolen hash, never knowing the cleartext password (ATT&CK [T1550.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/)).

MITRE ATT&CK lists reading LSASS memory as [T1003.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/) and notes it needs an administrator or SYSTEM. [Microsoft's own documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/attack-surface-reduction-rules-reference) names **Mimikatz**, a widely used credential extraction tool, as able to scrape cleartext passwords and NTLM hashes from LSASS when protections are off.

blocks.title: From one admin foothold to many machines

scenes.caption: Ana (an IT admin) signs in to a workstation. LSASS keeps credential material so Ana is not asked again.
An attacker who already has admin on this workstation opens lsass.exe and reads its memory.
The hash is enough for NTLM authentication. The attacker never needed Ana's password.
The attacker logs on to a server as Ana. The server's Security log shows a normal-looking network logon (type 3) for Ana.
With Credential Guard, the secrets live in an isolated process (LSAIso) protected by virtualization; admin malware in the normal OS cannot read them. Simplified.

blocks.md: **Real case: NotPetya (June 2017).** CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) reported that NotPetya's first and usually most effective way to spread was a **modified Mimikatz** stealing Windows credentials, which it then used with **WMIC** (the Windows Management Instrumentation command line) or **PsExec** to run itself on other machines. Another of its methods was the EternalBlue SMB exploit (plus EternalRomance, a second SMBv1 exploit). So machines patched against EternalBlue still fell when an admin's credentials were sitting in LSASS on an infected PC. NotPetya then encrypted files and, with admin rights, the MBR (master boot record, the first sector the PC boots from); researchers at Kaspersky, a Russian security company, showed [the victim ID was random](https://securelist.com/expetrpetyanotpetya-is-a-wiper-not-ransomware/78902/), so paying could never bring a key back.

**Defences, in layers:**
- **LSA protection** (`RunAsPPL`): runs LSASS as a **protected process**, so non-protected processes, even admin ones, cannot read its memory or inject code. Default on new Windows 11 22H2+ installs that are domain joined and meet hardware requirements.
- **Credential Guard**: uses **VBS** (virtualization-based security, a small isolated environment run by the hypervisor, which runs virtual machines) to keep NTLM hashes and Kerberos ticket-granting tickets out of reach; on by default on domain-joined Windows 11 22H2 and later systems that meet the requirements.
- **Attack surface reduction rule** "Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem" in Microsoft Defender, for machines that cannot use the first two.
- **Detection**: Sysmon (a free logging tool, lesson 12) event 10 (ProcessAccess) records which process opened LSASS; investigate anything that is not a known security or system tool.
- **Behaviour**: do not sign in to ordinary workstations with domain admin accounts, so their credentials are never there to steal.

blocks.code:
# Is LSA protection configured? (1 = on with UEFI lock, 2 = on without)
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name RunAsPPL
# Is it actually running protected? Look for WinInit event 12:
# "LSASS.exe was started as a protected process with level: 4"
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=12; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Wininit'} -MaxEvents 1

# Which processes opened lsass.exe recently? (needs Sysmon with a config
# that logs ProcessAccess, event 10)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id=10} -MaxEvents 200 |
  Where-Object Message -like '*lsass.exe*' |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Message
blocks.caption: Defensive, read-only checks.

blocks.question: An attacker has a standard (non-admin) user's shell on a laptop. Can they read LSASS memory to steal hashes?
options: Yes, any process can read any other process
Yes, because LSASS runs at low integrity
Not directly: reading LSASS memory requires administrator or SYSTEM, so they first need to escalate
Only if the user is in Remote Desktop Users
blocks.explain: ATT&CK notes LSASS credential material is harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM. That is why privilege escalation usually comes before credential dumping.

blocks.question: A server was fully patched against EternalBlue, yet NotPetya still infected it. According to CISA, what is the most likely route?
options: A zero-day in NTFS
Clearing the Security log
A UAC prompt the admin accepted
Credentials stolen from LSASS on another machine, then used with PsExec or WMIC
blocks.explain: CISA describes credential theft with a modified Mimikatz plus PsExec or WMIC as NotPetya's first and most effective method. Patches do not stop valid credentials.

lessons.title: The registry, Run keys and scheduled tasks: how programs come back

blocks.md:
The **registry** is a hierarchical database of settings that Windows and its programs need. It is a tree: each node is a **key** (like a folder), and keys hold **values** (a name, a type and data). Tools show it with paths like `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft`.

Tiny example: when you set dark mode, the choice is stored as a value under your user's part of the registry, and apps read it when they start.

The top-level **predefined keys** are always open; their names start with **HKEY**, the Windows type name for [a handle to a registry key](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winprog/windows-data-types). The ones you will use:
- **HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE** (HKLM): settings for the whole machine. Its subkeys include SAM, SECURITY, SOFTWARE and SYSTEM.
- **HKEY_CURRENT_USER** (HKCU): preferences of the user running the process.
- **HKEY_USERS** (HKU): the profiles currently loaded, usually the signed-in users and a few service accounts; a user who is not signed in has no hive here until their Ntuser.dat is loaded.

On disk the registry is split into **hives**: a hive is a group of keys and values backed by files that load into memory at boot or sign-in. Most hive files sit in `%SystemRoot%\System32\Config` (SAM, SECURITY, SOFTWARE, SYSTEM), and each user's HKCU comes from `Ntuser.dat` in their profile. The SAM hive holds local account data, so attackers with SYSTEM rights try to copy it, and defenders protect those files.

Why "hive"? Raymond Chen, a long-time Microsoft developer who writes the Old New Thing blog, [explains](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20030808-00/?p=42943) that one of the original Windows NT developers hated bees and slipped in bee references: registry files are hives, and registry data is stored in cells, like a honeycomb.

blocks.title: A Run key: one value makes a program start at every sign-in

scenes.caption: The path to a per-user Run key: HKCU, then Software, Microsoft, Windows, CurrentVersion, Run.
Each value under Run is a command line (up to 260 characters) that Windows runs when this user signs in. A legitimate sync client is a typical entry.
Malware adds its own value pointing to a file in the user's AppData. Writing to HKCU needs no admin rights: the user owns their own hive.
Sysmon event 13 (registry value set) records the write with the process that made it, and Autoruns lists every autostart entry for review.

blocks.md:
Windows reads four documented **Run and RunOnce** keys at sign-in: `Run` under both HKLM and HKCU runs its entries at every sign-in, and `RunOnce` deletes each entry and then runs it, so it runs once. ATT&CK lists this persistence trick as [T1547.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/). It is popular precisely because the per-user keys need no admin rights.

**Scheduled tasks** are the other classic way back in. The **Task Scheduler** runs programs at set times or on triggers such as sign-in or boot, under an account you choose. Attackers create tasks to rerun malware (ATT&CK [T1053.005](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/)). With the audit subcategory *Audit Other Object Access Events* enabled, the Security log writes **event 4698** every time a scheduled task is created.

blocks.code:
# Read (do not change) the four Run and RunOnce keys
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce'
Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce'

# Scheduled tasks outside Microsoft's own folder
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object TaskPath -NotLike '\Microsoft\*' |
  Select-Object TaskPath, TaskName, State
blocks.caption: Read-only hunting commands. In PowerShell the registry looks like a drive: HKLM: and HKCU:.

blocks.md: Autoruns, a free Sysinternals tool by Mark Russinovich (who created the Sysinternals site in 1996), shows every program configured to start at boot or sign-in, including Run keys, services and scheduled tasks, in one list. Comparing it against a known-good machine is a fast first triage step.

blocks.prompt: Malware writes a Run value under HKLM instead of HKCU. Compared with HKCU, what changes for the attacker and for you?
blocks.reveal: HKLM is machine-wide, so the entry runs for **every** user who signs in, not just one. Writing there normally needs administrator rights, so an HKLM entry also tells you the attacker already had admin. For hunting, check both: HKCU entries are per user, so on a shared machine look under each loaded user hive in HKEY_USERS too.

blocks.question: Which statement about RunOnce is correct according to Microsoft's documentation?
options: Its entries run at every sign-in forever
By default each value is deleted before its command runs, so it runs one time
It only works in Safe Mode
It requires a scheduled task to trigger it
blocks.explain: RunOnce values are deleted before the command runs by default (an exclamation mark prefix defers deletion until after). Run, without Once, repeats at every sign-in.

blocks.question: You want an alert whenever anyone creates a scheduled task on servers. What must be true for event 4698 to appear?
options: Nothing; 4698 is always on
Sysmon must be installed
The audit policy must enable the Audit Other Object Access Events subcategory
The task must run as SYSTEM
blocks.explain: 4698 belongs to the Audit Other Object Access Events subcategory. If that auditing is off, the Security log stays silent when tasks are created.

lessons.title: Event logs: anatomy of a record, and reading logons (4624, 4625)

blocks.md:
Windows has a central **event logging** service: programs and the operating system write **events** to named **logs** (also called channels), and the **Event Viewer** app or PowerShell reads them. The classic logs are **Application**, **System** (services, drivers) and **Security** (sign-ins, process creation, account changes). Many components have their own logs under *Applications and Services Logs*, such as `Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational` and `Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`.

Tiny example: when Ana signs in, the Security log gets an event with **Event ID 4624**, "an account was successfully logged on". The ID tells you the kind of event; the fields inside tell you who, from where and how.

What lands in the Security log is decided by the **audit policy**: categories such as Logon or Process Creation, each turned on for success, failure or both. If a subcategory is off, nothing is recorded, however bad the activity. `auditpol /get /category:*` lists the current policy.

Every event has a **System** part (provider, Event ID, time, computer, log) and an **EventData** part with named fields. Here is Microsoft's own sample of a 4624, trimmed.

blocks.code:
<Event>
  <System>
    <Provider Name="Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing" />
    <EventID>4624</EventID>
    <TimeCreated SystemTime="2015-11-12T00:24:35.079785200Z" />
    <Channel>Security</Channel>
    <Computer>WIN-GG82ULGC9GO</Computer>
  </System>
  <EventData>
    <Data Name="TargetUserSid">S-1-5-21-1377283216-344919071-3415362939-500</Data>
    <Data Name="TargetUserName">Administrator</Data>
    <Data Name="TargetLogonId">0x8dcdc</Data>
    <Data Name="LogonType">2</Data>
    <Data Name="AuthenticationPackageName">Negotiate</Data>
    <Data Name="WorkstationName">WIN-GG82ULGC9GO</Data>
    <Data Name="IpAddress">127.0.0.1</Data>
    <Data Name="ElevatedToken">%%1842</Data>
  </EventData>
</Event>
blocks.caption: Abridged from Microsoft's documentation for event 4624. TargetLogonId links this logon to later events from the same session.

blocks.md: The single most useful 4624 field is **Logon Type**: how the account arrived. The figure walks through the common ones. Two others in the table: type 7 (Unlock: a locked workstation was unlocked) and type 9 (NewCredentials: a process cloned its token and uses different credentials for outbound network connections while keeping the same local identity; unusual type 9 logons deserve a look).

blocks.title: 4624 logon types: how did this account get here?

scenes.caption: Logon types are numbers. Microsoft documents these values for 4624 (and 4625).
Type 2, interactive: someone signed in at this machine's keyboard and screen.
Type 3, network: a user or computer connected from the network, for example to a file share. Pass the hash and PsExec show up as type 3.
Type 5, service: the SCM started a service under an account. Type 4, batch: scheduled tasks run without a user present.
Type 10, RemoteInteractive: a Remote Desktop sign-in. Type 10 from an unexpected address is a classic alert.
Type 8 (NetworkCleartext) means the password reached this machine in unhashed form; type 11 means cached domain credentials were used with no domain controller contacted.

blocks.md:
**Failed sign-ins: [event 4625](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4625).** It is written on the machine where the attempt was made, with a **Status** and **Sub Status** code giving the reason. The codes Microsoft highlights:
- `0xC000006A`: right user name, bad password. Many in a row against one account suggests password guessing.
- `0xC0000064`: the user name does not exist. Many in a row suggests someone enumerating (listing) user names.
- `0xC0000072`: the account is disabled. Attempts on disabled accounts deserve a look.

**Event 4672** (special privileges assigned to new logon) follows the 4624 of any account holding powerful privileges such as SeDebugPrivilege, so it marks admin-level sign-ins.

blocks.title: 4625 failures by reason on one server (illustrative counts)

scenes.caption: A normal day: a few typos. Illustrative numbers for one server over one hour.
Mass 0xC0000064: someone is trying many user names that do not exist. User enumeration.
Then 0xC000006A against real names: password guessing on accounts that exist. Look for a 4624 from the same source address right after.

blocks.code:
# Last 50 successful and failed logons from the Security log (run as admin)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4624,4625} -MaxEvents 50 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message

# Remote Desktop logons only (logon type 10), using an XPath filter
Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -FilterXPath "*[System[EventID=4624] and EventData[Data[@Name='LogonType']='10']]" -MaxEvents 20
blocks.caption: Reading the Security log requires administrator rights.

blocks.question: A file server logs many 4625 events with Sub Status 0xC0000064 from one IP address, each for a different name. What is most likely happening?
options: Someone is trying user names that do not exist, enumerating accounts
An admin mistyped a password
A disabled account is in use
The server's clock is wrong
blocks.explain: 0xC0000064 means the user name does not exist. Many of them in a row is a sign of user enumeration, often followed by password guessing on the names that work.

blocks.question: Ana's account shows a 4624 with Logon Type 3 on a server Ana never uses, from Ana's workstation's IP address at 03:00. Why might this matter even though Ana's password was not typed?
options: Type 3 logons are always harmless
Type 3 means Ana was at the server's keyboard
Type 3 is only used by printers
A network logon can be made with stolen credential material such as an NTLM hash, so it fits credential theft on Ana's workstation
blocks.explain: Type 3 is a network logon. Pass the hash and remote admin tools produce exactly this, so an unusual type 3 at an odd hour is worth investigating alongside events on the source workstation.

lessons.title: Event IDs that tell an intrusion story: 4688, 4720, 7045, 1102

blocks.md:
Single events rarely prove anything; defenders read **sequences**. The IDs that turn up most in Windows investigations:

- **4688**: a new process was created (needs *Audit Process Creation*). The command line field stays **empty** unless the Group Policy setting "Include command line in process creation events" is on.
- **[4720](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4720)**: a user account was created.
- **4732**: a member was added to a security-enabled local group, for example Administrators.
- **4698**: a scheduled task was created.
- **7045** (System log, from the Service Control Manager): a service was installed. **4697** is the Security log's version and needs *Audit Security System Extension*.
- **4104** (PowerShell Operational log): a script block was logged.
- **1102**: the Security audit log was cleared.

Tiny example: creating a backdoor admin account produces 4720 then 4732 within seconds. Either alone may be routine; together at 03:00 on a server, they are not.

blocks.title: An illustrative intrusion, as the logs see it

scenes.caption: Minutes 0 to 6: dozens of failed network logons (4625, Sub Status 0xC000006A) against one account. Password guessing.
Minute 7: a successful network logon for the same account, followed by 4672: the account has admin privileges on this server.
Minute 12: a service is installed remotely (7045), the PsExec pattern, and 4688 shows the command shell it started.
Minutes 20 to 28: a PowerShell script block is logged (4104), then a new account appears (4720) and joins Administrators (4732). A backdoor account.
Minute 32: a scheduled task is created (4698) so the attacker's program comes back after a reboot.
Minute 55: the Security log is cleared, which itself writes 1102. Events already forwarded to a central collector survive, which is why logs must leave the machine.

blocks.md: **Why forward logs.** An attacker with admin rights on a machine can clear its logs. Clearing the Security log writes 1102, but the earlier events are gone from that machine. **WEF** (Windows Event Forwarding, built into Windows) or a **SIEM** agent (security information and event management: a central system that collects, searches and alerts on logs) copies events off the machine as they happen. Microsoft's own WEF guidance subscribes to exactly the events above: 1102, 4720 and related account events, 7045, and PowerShell 4104.

blocks.code:
<Event>
  <System>
    <EventID>4688</EventID>
    <Channel>Security</Channel>
    <Computer>WIN-GG82ULGC9GO.contoso.local</Computer>
  </System>
  <EventData>
    <Data Name="NewProcessId">0x2bc</Data>
    <Data Name="NewProcessName">C:\Windows\System32\rundll32.exe</Data>
    <Data Name="TokenElevationType">%%1938</Data>
    <Data Name="CommandLine" />
    <Data Name="TargetUserName">dadmin</Data>
    <Data Name="ParentProcessName">C:\Windows\explorer.exe</Data>
    <Data Name="MandatoryLabel">S-1-16-8192</Data>
  </EventData>
</Event>
blocks.caption: Abridged from Microsoft's sample 4688. Note the empty CommandLine: the policy to include it was off. Process ID 0x2bc is 700 in decimal, as Task Manager shows it.

blocks.md: Turn on command-line logging for 4688 (or deploy Sysmon). Without it you know rundll32.exe ran, but not what it was told to do, and that is usually the part that matters.

blocks.code:
# New services from the System log, using the same filter Microsoft's WEF guide uses
Get-WinEvent -LogName System -FilterXPath "*[System[Provider[@Name='Service Control Manager'] and (EventID=7045)]]" -MaxEvents 20

# Account created, added to a local group, task created, log cleared
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4720,4732,4698,1102} -MaxEvents 50 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
blocks.caption: Run as administrator on your own lab machine.

blocks.question: An attacker clears the Security log on a server. What does a defender who only looks at that server's Security log afterwards see?
options: Nothing at all, so the attack is invisible
A 1102 event recording that the log was cleared, and only events written after it
Every old event, because clearing is undone at reboot
A 4720 event
blocks.explain: Clearing writes 1102, so the clear itself is visible. The older events are gone locally, which is why forwarding to a central collector matters.

blocks.question: A 4688 event shows `powershell.exe` started by `winword.exe`, but the CommandLine field is empty. What is the most likely reason?
options: The Group Policy setting to include command lines in process creation events is not enabled
PowerShell never has a command line
The event was forged
Word processes cannot pass arguments
blocks.explain: By default 4688's Process Command Line is empty; Microsoft documents that the Include command line in process creation events policy must be enabled.

blocks.question: Which pair of events, close together, most strongly suggests a backdoor administrator account was created?
options: 4720 then 4732 (added to Administrators)
blocks.explain: 4720 is account creation and 4732 is a member added to a security-enabled local group. Together they describe a new account being made a local admin.

lessons.title: Sysmon and Microsoft Defender: deeper telemetry, built-in defence

blocks.md:
The Security log was designed for auditing, not hunting. **Sysmon** (System Monitor), a free Sysinternals tool by Mark Russinovich and Thomas Garnier, fills the gaps. It installs as a Windows service plus a driver, survives reboots, and writes detailed events to `Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`. Its service runs as a protected process, which blocks many user-mode attempts to tamper with it.

Tiny example: where 4688 tells you `rundll32.exe` started, Sysmon event 1 also gives the full command line, a hash of the file and a **ProcessGuid**, a unique ID that lets you follow this exact process across all later events.

Sysmon event IDs worth knowing:
- **1** process creation (command line, hashes, parent)
- **3** network connection, linked to the process (disabled by default; enable it in the config)
- **10** process access: one process opening another. The documented use case is spotting tools that read LSASS memory.
- **11** file created or overwritten, useful for autostart folders
- **12, 13, 14** registry: 12 key and value create and delete, 13 value set, 14 key and value rename (Run keys show up here)
- **22** DNS query made by a process

What Sysmon records is controlled by an XML **configuration** file passed at install time (`sysmon64 -accepteula -i config.xml`). Community templates such as [sysmon-config by SwiftOnSecurity, a pseudonymous security writer,](https://github.com/SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config) are common starting points; tune them so the volume stays manageable. Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 now also ship Sysmon as a built-in optional feature, updated through Windows Update; it cannot run alongside the standalone download.

blocks.title: Where Windows telemetry comes from, and where it goes

scenes.caption: Four sources on one endpoint: the Security log, Sysmon, the PowerShell log and the Defender Antivirus log.
A forwarder (Windows Event Forwarding or a SIEM agent) copies events off the machine as they are written.
The SIEM stores, searches and correlates: 4625 bursts, 7045 on servers, Sysmon 10 against lsass.exe, Defender 5001.
An analyst gets an alert with context from several sources at once, even if the attacker later clears the endpoint's logs.

blocks.md:
**Microsoft Defender Antivirus** is built into Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server. Beyond signatures it uses machine learning, cloud lookups and behaviour monitoring. Its events go to `Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Windows Defender > Operational`:
- **1116**: malware or potentially unwanted software detected.
- **1117**: action taken (quarantined, removed).
- **5001**: real-time protection was **disabled**.
- **5007**: configuration changed; Microsoft notes an unexpected 5007 might be the result of malware.

Attackers often try to switch protection off first. **Tamper protection** prevents important security settings from being disabled or changed. **AMSI** (from lesson 2) lets PowerShell, Windows Script Host and Office macros pass content to Defender before it runs, and **attack surface reduction (ASR) rules** block risky behaviours such as reading LSASS memory.

blocks.title: AMSI: a script is scanned before it runs

scenes.caption: A script, perhaps decoded from an obfuscated string, reaches the PowerShell engine.
Before executing, PowerShell hands the actual code to AMSI. Decoding has already happened, so the scanner sees plain code.
AMSI forwards it to the installed antimalware product, here Defender, which returns a verdict.
The script does not run and Defender logs the detection and action. Simplified: details vary by configuration.

blocks.code:
# Defender status (read-only)
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMRunningMode, AMServiceEnabled, AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled

# Detections, actions, and protection being turned off
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational'; Id=1116,1117,5001,5007} -MaxEvents 50 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message

# Sysmon process creations (if Sysmon is installed)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id=1} -MaxEvents 20
blocks.caption: AMRunningMode shows Normal when Defender is the active antivirus, Passive when another product is primary.

blocks.question: You want to know which program opened lsass.exe at 02:10 last night. Which source is designed for that?
options: Security event 4720
Defender event 5007
System event 7045
Sysmon event 10 (ProcessAccess)
blocks.explain: Sysmon's ProcessAccess event records one process opening another, and Microsoft's documentation names reading LSASS memory as the use case. It needs a config that includes it, with filters for noise.

blocks.question: A laptop's Defender log shows event 5001 at 03:12, followed by no detections all night. How should you read that?
options: Good news: no malware was detected
Suspicious: real-time protection was disabled, so the quiet night may mean nothing was being checked
Normal: 5001 is a daily heartbeat
It means Sysmon stopped
blocks.explain: 5001 means real-time protection was disabled. Silence after it is not evidence of safety. Tamper protection exists to stop exactly this.

lessons.title: SMB file shares and EternalBlue: how WannaCry spread

blocks.md:
**SMB** (Server Message Block) is the Windows network file-sharing protocol: it lets a program read, create and update files on a remote server over TCP/IP. It uses **TCP port 445**. When you open `\\fileserver\finance`, that is SMB, and the server logs a network logon (4624 type 3) for you.

Tiny example: `Get-SmbShare` on a Windows machine lists its shares. Besides the folders people share on purpose you will see default administrative shares: `ADMIN` (the Windows folder, "Remote Admin"), `C` (the C: drive, "Default share") and `IPC` ("Remote IPC"), each with a dollar sign at the end of its name. Remote admin tools like PsExec copy their service program through these shares.

SMB has versions. **SMBv1** is the original, and Microsoft says it "has significant security vulnerabilities, and we strongly encourage you not to use it". It is not installed by default in Windows 11, Windows Server 2019 and later, or Windows 10 except Home and Pro editions. SMBv2 and SMBv3 add features such as encryption (SMB 3) and stronger signing; since Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025, SMB signing is required by default.

**EternalBlue.** On 14 March 2017 Microsoft published security bulletin **MS17-010**, fixing bugs that allowed remote code execution if an attacker sent specially crafted messages to an SMBv1 server. On 14 April 2017 a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers published an exploit for it codenamed **EternalBlue**. Systems that had installed the March patch were safe from it; many had not.

**WannaCry (12 May 2017)** was **ransomware** (malware that encrypts files and demands payment) that also behaved as a **worm** (malware that spreads by itself, with no user clicking anything). Recall the story from security-basics; here is the Windows view. [CISA reported](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2017/05/12/indicators-associated-wannacry-ransomware) that its dropper (the first program that runs and installs the rest) installed itself as an auto-start **service named mssecsvc2.0**, so the System log got a 7045, then scanned the local network on UDP 137 and 138 and TCP 139 and 445 and used EternalBlue on machines that answered on 445. Before doing anything, it tried to reach a hard-coded, unregistered web domain and [exited if the domain answered](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/wannacry-malware-profile/); Marcus Hutchins, a security researcher who blogged as MalwareTech, [registered that domain](https://www.malwaretech.com/2017/05/how-to-accidentally-stop-a-global-cyber-attacks.html), which acted as a kill switch.

Recall from security-basics the UK National Audit Office (NAO) findings on the NHS: dozens of hospital trusts and hundreds of GP practices hit. Every infected organisation shared the same weakness: unpatched or unsupported Windows. The NAO adds that managing internet-facing firewalls would have protected them even without the patch.

blocks.title: How a worm moves over SMB (simplified)

scenes.caption: WannaCry first checks its kill-switch domain. In the first hours the domain did not exist, so the malware carried on.
It scans for anything answering on TCP 445. This machine still runs SMBv1 and lacks MS17-010.
The crafted messages trigger the bug and run the worm's code on the target with no user involved. The target starts scanning too.
A machine with MS17-010 installed, or SMBv1 removed, is not infected by this route.
After the researcher registered the domain, new infections found it reachable and exited before encrypting.

blocks.code:
# Is the SMBv1 server protocol enabled? (False is what you want)
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object EnableSMB1Protocol

# Is the SMBv1 feature installed at all?
Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol

# Remove it (elevated). Test first: very old devices may still need SMBv1.
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol

# Which shares does this machine offer?
Get-SmbShare
blocks.caption: Commands from Microsoft's SMB documentation. Before removing SMBv1, you can audit who still uses it with the AuditSmb1Access setting.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**
- **Prevent**: install security updates promptly (MS17-010 was out two months before WannaCry), remove SMBv1, and block SMB at the network boundary: CISA advised blocking TCP 445 plus related UDP 137 and 138 and TCP 139. Workstations rarely need to accept SMB from other workstations, so host firewalls can block it internally too.
- **Detect**: a workstation suddenly connecting to TCP 445 on hundreds of addresses is worm-like scanning (Sysmon event 3, firewall logs). New services named after remote tools (7045) and type 3 logons from unusual sources follow successful spread.
- **Respond**: isolate infected machines from the network first, because a worm spreads faster than people can clean.

Worms need two things: a reachable service and a bug in it. Patching removes the bug; turning off SMBv1 and blocking 445 removes the reachability. Do both, because you will never patch everything on time.

blocks.question: According to the NAO, what would have protected NHS organisations from WannaCry even if they had not patched?
options: Paying the ransom quickly
Renaming the Administrator account
Managing their internet-facing firewalls
Turning on script block logging
blocks.explain: The NAO report says that whether or not systems were patched, managing internet-facing firewalls would have guarded organisations against infection. Reachability matters as much as the bug.

blocks.question: Why could WannaCry spread inside a network with nobody opening an email?
options: It was a worm: it scanned for SMB on TCP 445 and exploited unpatched SMBv1 servers directly
It guessed user passwords over RDP
It used a UAC bypass
It was installed by Windows Update
blocks.explain: The EternalBlue exploit needs only network access to a vulnerable SMBv1 server. No user action is required on the target, which is what makes it wormable.

lessons.title: Remote Desktop and BlueKeep: logons before login

blocks.md:
**RDP** (Remote Desktop Protocol) lets you control a Windows PC from another device as if you sat at it. Pro, Enterprise, Education and Server editions can host it (Home editions cannot). Sessions start on **TCP port 3389**. Accounts must be allowed: by default members of Administrators and of the **Remote Desktop Users** group, and an RDP sign-in shows up as a 4624 with **logon type 10** (RemoteInteractive).

Tiny example: an admin connects from home to a server over a VPN. The server logs 4624 type 10 for the admin's account with the VPN address as source. The same event from an address in another country at 04:00 is an incident.

**NLA** (Network Level Authentication) makes users authenticate **before** the remote session is set up. Without NLA, the server starts building a session, and runs a lot of code, for anyone who connects. That matters because of bugs like BlueKeep.

**BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708)** was a remote code execution bug in Remote Desktop Services patched in **May 2019**. It affected Windows 2000, XP, Vista, 7, Server 2003 and Server 2008 (and R2). An attacker could send specially crafted packets to a machine with RDP enabled and run code with **no authentication and no user interaction**, which CISA called **wormable**, like WannaCry. The root cause, [analysed by the Zero Day Initiative](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/blog/2019/5/27/cve-2019-0708-a-comprehensive-analysis-of-a-remote-desktop-services-vulnerability) (Trend Micro's vulnerability research programme), was a **use-after-free** in the RDP kernel driver `termdd.sys`: a client could bind an internal channel named `MS_T120`, the server freed that channel's structure on error, and later wrote to the freed memory. A use-after-free means a program keeps using memory after giving it back, so whoever controls what fills that memory next can steer the program.

Microsoft took the unusual step of also patching out-of-support systems (XP, Vista, Server 2003).

blocks.title: Why NLA blunts a pre-authentication bug (simplified)

scenes.caption: An unpatched Windows 7 server without NLA accepts the connection and starts setting up a session for an unknown client.
The bug lives in that setup code, so it can be triggered before any password is asked for. No account is needed.
With NLA, the server demands valid credentials before creating the session.
Without credentials the attacker never reaches the vulnerable code. An attacker who has valid credentials still could, so patching remains essential.

blocks.md:
**CISA's mitigations for BlueKeep:** install the patches; upgrade end-of-life systems; disable services you do not use; **enable NLA**, which "effectively mitigates" BlueKeep because exploitation needs an unauthenticated session; and **block TCP 3389 at the perimeter firewall**, noting that this does not stop attacks from inside the network.

Beyond BlueKeep, internet-exposed RDP attracts constant password guessing. Put RDP behind a VPN or gateway, require strong authentication, keep the Remote Desktop Users group small, and alert on bursts of 4625 on RDP hosts and on type 10 logons from unusual addresses. With NLA on (the default), a failed RDP sign-in is logged as 4625 with logon type **3**, not 10, because the password is checked over the network before any session exists, so a type 10 filter misses most guessing.

blocks.code:
# Who may sign in over Remote Desktop?
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Remote Desktop Users'

# Successful RDP logons (type 10) in the Security log
Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -FilterXPath "*[System[EventID=4624] and EventData[Data[@Name='LogonType']='10']]" -MaxEvents 20 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Message

# Failed logons, network (3) or RemoteInteractive (10). With NLA on,
# failed RDP sign-ins appear as type 3, so include both.
Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -FilterXPath "*[System[EventID=4625] and EventData[Data[@Name='LogonType']='3' or Data[@Name='LogonType']='10']]" -MaxEvents 50
blocks.caption: Read-only. Run as administrator.

blocks.question: A Windows Server 2008 R2 machine cannot be patched this week. Which single setting does CISA say effectively mitigates BlueKeep, and why?
options: Renaming port 3389
Turning on script block logging
Adding users to Remote Desktop Users
Enabling Network Level Authentication, because exploitation needs an unauthenticated session
blocks.explain: With NLA the session is only set up after authentication, and BlueKeep must be triggered in an unauthenticated session. Patching is still required, since an attacker with credentials is not stopped.

blocks.question: Which Security log entry is the normal record of a successful Remote Desktop sign-in?
options: 4624 with logon type 2
4624 with logon type 10
blocks.explain: Logon type 10 is RemoteInteractive: Terminal Services or Remote Desktop. Type 2 is a sign-in at the machine's own console.

lessons.title: Patch Tuesday and PrintNightmare: closing holes on a schedule

blocks.md:
Microsoft ships its [monthly security update](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/deployment/update/release-cycle) on the **second Tuesday of each month**, typically at 10:00 AM Pacific Time. People call it **Patch Tuesday** (also Update Tuesday, or "B week" because it lands in the second week). The updates are **cumulative**: each one contains all previous security fixes, so a machine that installs the latest one is caught up. Organisations deliver them through Windows Update, WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) and other management tools.

Tiny example: if a fix ships on Tuesday 9 June and your servers update on the following Saturday, your exposure window for that bug is four days, provided attackers did not know about it before Tuesday.

The predictable date cuts both ways. Defenders can plan testing and rollout; researchers and attackers can study what a patch changed to locate the bug, by comparing the old and new files (patch diffing). The Zero Day Initiative write-up from the last lesson, for example, names the two termdd.sys functions the BlueKeep patch fixed, IcaBindVirtualChannels and IcaReBindVirtualChannels. The 2017 sequence shows the gap that matters: not the time until Microsoft ships a fix, but the time until **you install it**.

blocks.title: 2017: one patch, three outbreaks (days after 14 March)

scenes.caption: Day 0, 14 March 2017: Microsoft publishes MS17-010 for the SMBv1 bugs, rated Critical.
Day 31, 14 April: the Shadow Brokers publish EternalBlue. Anyone can now attack machines that skipped the March patch.
Day 59, 12 May: WannaCry spreads worldwide through unpatched SMBv1 machines.
Day 105, 27 June: NotPetya uses EternalBlue too, plus stolen credentials. Over three months after the fix shipped, unpatched machines were still there.

blocks.md:
**PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527, 2021).** The **Print Spooler** is the Windows service that manages printing, and it runs as SYSTEM, even on domain controllers (the servers that run a company's Active Directory). CISA describes the bug: the spooler "improperly performs privileged file operations and fails to restrict access to functionality that allows users to add printers and related drivers", so a remote **authenticated** attacker, meaning any ordinary domain user, could run code as **SYSTEM**. On a domain controller that means control of the whole organisation's identity system.
