CISA treated it as an emergency. **Emergency Directive 21-04** (13 July 2021) required US federal agencies to stop **and disable** the spooler on all domain controllers by 14 July, install the July 2021 cumulative updates by 20 July, and on other machines either disable the spooler or restrict printer driver installation to administrators.

blocks.title: PrintNightmare in one picture, and the fix

scenes.caption: Any signed-in domain user can talk to the Print Spooler service, which runs as SYSTEM.
The bug: the spooler lets that user add a printer driver, and the driver code then runs inside a SYSTEM process.
Fix 1: install the July 2021 cumulative update (and later ones).
Fix 2: restrict driver installation to administrators (RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators = 1), so the user's request is refused.
Fix 3, best on domain controllers: disable the spooler entirely. A service that is not running cannot be exploited.

blocks.code:
# Is the Print Spooler running, and how does it start?
Get-Service -Name Spooler | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

# On a domain controller that does not print: stop AND disable it (elevated).
# Stopping alone is not enough: the service would start again at reboot.
Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force
Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled

# Check the driver-install restriction from CISA ED 21-04 (1 = admins only)
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint' -Name RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators
blocks.caption: CISA's directive stresses that stopping the service without disabling it does not survive a reboot.

blocks.md: Attack surface reduction: every service running as SYSTEM is a door. If a machine does not need a service (printing on a domain controller, SMBv1 anywhere, RDP on the internet), turn it off. You cannot be exploited through code that is not running.

blocks.question: A domain controller never prints. A new Print Spooler bug is announced but the patch is a week away. What is the strongest immediate step?
options: Stop and disable the spooler service
Stop the spooler service now and restart it after patching
Rename the spooler service
Turn on 4688 command-line logging
blocks.explain: A disabled service cannot be reached, and disabling (not just stopping) survives reboots. That is exactly what CISA's ED 21-04 required for domain controllers.

blocks.question: MS17-010 shipped on 14 March 2017; WannaCry hit on 12 May. What does that gap teach?
options: Microsoft was too slow to patch
Patches cause outbreaks
The window that matters is between a fix's release and its installation; organisations that patched within weeks were not hit by this route
Cumulative updates skip older fixes
blocks.explain: The fix existed 59 days before WannaCry. The machines that fell were the ones that had not installed it, which is why patch speed is a core security metric.

lessons.title: First look at domains and Active Directory

blocks.md:
So far each computer kept its own accounts in its own SAM. With 5,000 laptops that does not scale: you would create Ana 5,000 times. A **domain** solves this. Computers **join** the domain and trust a central directory for accounts, groups and policy.

[AD DS](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/get-started/virtual-dc/active-directory-domain-services-overview) (Active Directory Domain Services) is Microsoft's directory service: a hierarchical store of objects on the network, such as user and computer accounts, groups, servers and printers, plus the rules to find and secure them. The servers that hold it are **domain controllers** (DCs). Every DC holds a copy of the directory, and with one username and password Ana can sign in to any domain-joined machine and reach resources across the network.

Tiny example: Ana signs in to a shared meeting-room PC Ana has never used. It works because the PC asks a domain controller, not its own SAM.

Domain accounts have SIDs too. The domain identifier now names the domain, and the RID names the account. Every domain has a **Domain Admins** group with RID 512, for example `S-1-5-21-1004336348-1177238915-682003330-512` in Microsoft's example domain Contoso. Members of Domain Admins can control every machine in the domain, which makes the group, and the DCs themselves, the main prize for attackers.

Two authentication protocols matter:
- [Kerberos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/kerberos-authentication-overview) (version 5, an industry standard; RFC 4120 says the name comes from the three-headed dog that guards Hades in Greek myth): three parties, the client, the service and the **KDC** (Key Distribution Center) that both trust, which runs on every DC. The client first gets a **TGT** (ticket-granting ticket) and then trades it for **service tickets**, so the password is not sent again for each service.
- **NTLM**: the older challenge-response family from the LSASS lesson, still used when Kerberos cannot be.

blocks.title: Kerberos in four messages (simplified)

scenes.caption: At sign-in, Ana's PC proves Ana's identity to the KDC on a domain controller.
The KDC returns a ticket-granting ticket. The PC caches it until it expires. Credential Guard protects these TGTs.
To reach file server FS01, the PC shows the TGT and gets a service ticket for that one service.
FS01 can verify the ticket itself and grants access; a network logon (type 3) appears in FS01's Security log.

blocks.md:
**Group Policy** is how one admin configures thousands of machines. Settings are bundled into a **GPO** (Group Policy Object) stored in AD and applied to computers and users. Almost every defence in this course is deployed this way: audit policy, command-line logging for 4688, script block logging, LSA protection, UAC behaviour, disabling SMBv1 or the spooler. That also means a GPO is powerful for attackers who gain control of one.

**Windows LAPS** (from lesson 3) is a domain feature too: it gives each machine's local admin a unique, rotating password stored in AD, so one stolen local password does not open every machine.

**Real case: NotPetya at Maersk.** NotPetya spread with stolen credentials and EternalBlue and destroyed machines across the shipping company Maersk's network, including its domain controllers. [Wired's reconstruction](https://www.wired.com/story/notpetya-cyberattack-ukraine-russia-code-crashed-the-world/) reports that Maersk's IT staff eventually found one surviving domain controller in an office in Ghana, which had been offline because of a power cut and so held the only untouched copy of the domain data. Maersk's chairman later said it took about ten days to rebuild **4,000 servers and 45,000 PCs**; Wired notes full recovery took close to two months.

The lessons for defenders: the domain controllers are the crown jewels, so protect them like it (few admins, no browsing or email on them, unneeded services such as the spooler disabled) and keep **offline** backups of AD that an attacker on the network cannot reach. Kerberos attacks, AD permissions and attack paths are covered in later courses.

blocks.question: Why do attackers who land on one workstation in a domain usually aim for Domain Admins rather than staying local?
options: Local admin rights do not exist in a domain
Domain Admins accounts have no SID
Kerberos is turned off for local accounts only
Domain Admins members can control every machine in the domain, so one account gives the whole network
blocks.explain: Domain Admins (RID 512) can administer every domain-joined machine and the DCs. Getting there turns one foothold into control of the organisation.

blocks.question: Maersk's recovery depended on one domain controller that was offline during the attack. What defensive practice does that point to?
options: Keeping RDP open on DCs for faster recovery
Keeping offline, unreachable backups of Active Directory
Running more domain controllers on the same network
Disabling Kerberos
blocks.explain: Every online DC replicated with or was reachable by the malware. Only an offline copy survived. Offline backups of AD are a core resilience control.

blocks.md: **Practise legally.** Build a small lab you own: a Windows virtual machine (and later a test domain controller), install Sysmon with a community config, and run the read-only commands from this course. Then generate events yourself (create a user, add it to a group, install a test service) and find them with `Get-WinEvent`. For recorded data from simulated attacks, the [OTRF Security-Datasets](https://github.com/OTRF/Security-Datasets) project publishes Windows event logs you can replay and search. For guided practice, Hack The Box Academy's [Windows Fundamentals](https://academy.hackthebox.com/course/preview/windows-fundamentals) and [Windows Event Logs and Finding Evil](https://academy.hackthebox.com/course/preview/windows-event-logs--finding-evil) modules, and the investigations on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/), cover this material.
